tagline: The far end of Maine's longest state road, up the Fish.
intro: From Fort Kent on the St. John, Route 11 heads south up the valley of the Fish River, which comes north out of Portage Lake through St. Froid Lake and Eagle Lake to meet the St. John at town. The road keeps roughly to the river the whole way to Portage Lake.

This stretch was Maine's first scenic byway. It is now the Fish River part of a national byway, joined at Fort Kent to the state's first cultural byway along the St. John, where French is heard as often as English. The highway itself starts 400 miles back, at the New Hampshire line. These are its last miles, or its first.

moments.title: Fort Kent
moments.text: The village began in 1839 with a blockhouse built for the Aroostook War and named for Governor Edward Kent, and it still stands where the Fish meets the St. John.

moments.title: Eagle Lake
moments.text: The lake is shaped like an L, takes the Fish River in at the bend, and lets it out again 13 miles above Fort Kent.

moments.title: Portage Lake
moments.text: Lumbermen from Canada settled here in 1844, the town took the lake's French name for carrying, and Route 11 is still the only state road it has.
